variables_mentioned: hours of work lost due to holidays on weekdays

treatment and instrument (income information used to simulate marginal taxes)
treatment and instrument (income information used to simulate marginal taxes)
controls (workplace controls); reference population of all employments for the LON coverage comparison

linkages: Individuals are followed over time in a long panel and their register records (hours from LON, income from IND/INDK/INPI, workplace from IDAN, demographics from BEF/FAIN/FAMILIE, education from UDDA) are combined at the individual level.
Hours of work are summed over all employments of an individual in a year, so secondary employment is included.
Employments in LON are compared with IDAN (which contains all employments) in Table A.2 to document coverage.
Municipality of residence links individuals to municipal tax rates and to the municipal unemployment rate.

sample.universe: Danish wage earners aged 25-65 observed in the administrative registers over 2002-2016 (the period is restricted to 2002 onwards because contract hours in LON are only available from 2002).
sample.unit_of_observation: individual-year (base year t), with three-year differences between t and t+3
selection_rules: all information needed to calculate marginal taxes available
neither jobless nor outside the labor force as a primary occupation as of the end of November at time t
strictly positive performed hours of work at both t and t+s (s = 3 in the main specification)
non-missing three-year change in the log marginal net-of-tax rate; more than one observation in the sample period (initial sample: 11,757,144 observations, Table A.1 Column (1))
base-year labor income greater than 250,000 DKK (2015 level) (10,874,515 observations, Table A.1 Column (2))

all variables included in the main regression (Column (4) of Table 2) non-missing, which requires the individual to be observed for several periods because of the twice-lagged income controls (10,755,733 observations, Table A.1 Column (3))
sample.n_observations: 10,755,733 in the main estimation sample (11,757,144 before the income and non-missing restrictions)

construction_notes: Performed hours of work: h = h^c + h^o - h^a - Vacation - Holiday hours (Eq. (5) and Eq. (7)), summed over all employments per individual-year.
The vacation-hours variable in LON is missing for 2009 and after but is approximately imputed using the remaining hour components and Eq. (7).
Statistics Denmark imputes values for firms reporting implausibly low paid absence.
Hours are transformed from annual to approximately weekly in the descriptive tables and figures by multiplying by 7/365.

Marginal taxes: tau_it = [T_t(z_it + 100) - T_t(z_it)]/100, computed with tax simulation programs originally developed by Kleven and Schultz (2014) and expanded by the Danish Ministry of Finance (available 1984-2016).
Instruments: Delta_s ln(1 - tau^p_{it,t-k}) = ln(1 - T'_{t+s}(z_{it-k})) - ln(1 - T'_t(z_{it-k})) (Eq. (2)); k = 2 in the main specification.
Income controls: ten-piece spline of log labor income with breakpoints at the deciles, lagged k years.
All monetary variables deflated to 2015 levels using the CPI from Statistics Denmark.
Main specification uses three-year differences (s = 3); differences of 1 to 6 years are reported in Table B.2.

LON covers approximately 50 % of main employments in Denmark; all public employers and firms with 100+ employees report, private firms with 10-100 employees are sampled, and private firms with fewer than 10 full-time equivalent employees are not part of LON.

links.pointer_quote: First, I estimate the three-year ELS, ELI (elasticity of labor income), and ETI (elasticity of taxable income) to be 0.08, 0.06, and 0.1, respectively.

claims.statement: An increase in the marginal net-of-tax rate on additional labor income increases performed hours of work over three years: the uncompensated intensive-margin elasticity of labor supply is estimated at 0.0814.

treatment.label: Delta ln(1 - tau): three-year log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate on additional labor income

register_source.value: IND, INDK and INPI (income information used to simulate marginal taxes)

definition.value: tau_it is the marginal tax rate on additional labor income, calculated as tau_it = [T_t(z_it + 100) - T_t(z_it)]/100 with tax simulation programs from Kleven and Schultz (2014) expanded by the Danish Ministry of Finance; the regressor is Delta_s ln(1 - tau_it) = ln(1 - tau_{it+s}) - ln(1 - tau_it) with s = 3, instrumented by the predicted mechanical change of Eq. (2) evaluated at income lagged k = 2 years.

timing.value: three-year change from base year t to t+3; the instrument uses income information from t-2

outcome.label: Delta ln h: three-year log change in performed hours of work

register_source.value: LON (Lønstatistikken)

definition.value: Performed hours of work h = h^c + h^o - h^a - Vacation - Holiday hours (Eq. (5)), summed over hours of performed work in all employments in a year per individual; the outcome is the 3-year log change ln h_{t+3} - ln h_t.

timing.value: change between year t and year t+3

units.value: elasticity: log change in performed hours of work per unit log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate (1 - tau)

magnitude.interpretation: The paper reads the estimate of 0.08 as implying that a decrease in the marginal tax rate of 10 % leads to an increase in labor supply of about 0.8 % at the intensive margin.

estimand.target_population: Danish wage earners aged 25-65 observed in the administrative registers 2002-2016, not jobless or outside the labor force as primary occupation at the end of November in t and t+s, with strictly positive performed hours of work in t and t+s, base-year labor income above 250,000 DKK (2015 level) and non-missing control variables.
estimand.compliers: Taxpayers whose marginal net-of-tax rate moved with the mechanical change implied by the 2003, 2007, 2009 and 2012 reforms given their twice-lagged labor income; the paper notes the compliant population changes with the instrument lag.
estimand.time_horizon: three-year change, from base year t to t+3

population.description: Danish wage earners aged 25-65 observed in the administrative registers 2002-2016, not jobless or outside the labor force as primary occupation at the end of November in t and t+s, with strictly positive performed hours of work in t and t+s, base-year labor income above 250,000 DKK (2015 level) and non-missing control variables.
population.selection: Hours of work are observed only for employments covered by LON, which covers approximately 50 % of main employments in Denmark (all public employers and all firms with 100+ employees, sampled private firms with 10-100 employees); workers in LON have higher average labor and taxable income than in IDAN. The sample is further conditioned on employment with strictly positive performed hours at t and t+s (intensive margin only), on base-year labor income above 250,000 DKK (2015 level) and on non-missing controls, including twice-lagged income.

identification.source_of_variation: The 2003, 2007, 2009 and 2012 Danish tax reforms over the period 2002-2016 (mainly changes to the middle- and top-bracket thresholds and the abolition of the middle-bracket tax in 2010), plus annual municipal tax changes; the exogenous component is the mechanical change in the marginal net-of-tax rate that the new tax system implies for an individual's income lagged k years (Eq. (2)).
identification.instrument: Delta ln(1 - tau^p_{it,t-2}): the predicted (mechanical) three-year change in the log marginal net-of-tax rate, computed by applying the tax systems of years t and t+3 to labor income of year t-2 (Eq. (2), k = 2)

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument validity: the covariance between the predicted (mechanical) change in the log net-of-tax rate and the error term of the hours equation is small (zero in the limit), so the instrument affects hours of work only through the actual change in the marginal net-of-tax rate.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Eq. (3)-(4); graphical inspection of mean reversion (Fig. B.1); difference-in-Sargan overidentification tests in Table B.6, where exogeneity of the main instrument is not rejected for P-values below 30 %.

implies_edges.from: Delta_s ln(1 - tau^p_{it,t-k}): predicted (mechanical) change in the log marginal net-of-tax rate, Eq. (2)
implies_edges.to: Delta ln h: three-year log change in performed hours of work

formal.as_written: plim(e^IV) = e + cov[Delta_s ln(1 - tau^p_{it,t-k}), nu_it | v_it] / cov[Delta_s ln(1 - tau^p_{it,t-k}), Delta_s ln(1 - tau_it) | v_it] (Eq. (3)); validity requires |cov[Delta_s ln(1 - tau^p_{it,t-k}), nu_it | v_it]| small

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: the predicted (mechanical) change in the log net-of-tax rate is strongly correlated with the actual change in the log marginal net-of-tax rate.
key_assumptions.supported_by: first-stage F-statistics reported in every table and in Table B.1; the paper states they are in all cases above the levels advised to avoid weak instruments.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on individual, year and municipality fixed effects, socioeconomic controls and a ten-piece spline of log labor income lagged two years, the instrument is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of hours growth, i.e. mean reversion and heterogeneous growth rates in hours of work across income levels are absorbed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: graphical inspection of the correlation between initial labor income and the three-year change in hours (Fig. B.1a), which the paper says almost entirely disappears after lagging initial labor income twice; sensitivity of the estimate to income controls in Table B.4.

different instrument and income-control lag lengths k = 0 to 4 (Table B.3)

heterogeneity.finding: Fig. 3 reveals strong heterogeneity by gender: men have a baseline elasticity of about 0.05 and women about 0.14.

Fig. 3 reveals strong heterogeneity by education; the paper attributes it partly to lower education levels being associated with lower earnings, which were less targeted by the reforms, and to varying precision of performed hours by education.
Relatively young individuals are estimated to be more responsive than older individuals.
Individuals with young children in the household are more responsive than those without, but with considerable uncertainty in the estimates.
Heterogeneity is otherwise limited and all elasticity estimates are modest, below 0.2.

evidence.how: The table legend defines * p<0.1, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01; the p-value recorded is the threshold implied by the stars printed on this coefficient, not an exact p-value.

Both sides of Eq. (1) are log changes, so the coefficient on Delta ln(1 - tau) is an elasticity of the dependent variable with respect to the marginal net-of-tax rate; the paper calls it the uncompensated elasticity of labor supply.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of the reform, hours of work at reform-targeted income levels would have followed the same trend as at untargeted income levels, so the difference in three-year hours changes between the reform and pre-reform periods identifies the reform effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Panel (c) of Fig. 2 and Fig. B.2 show changes in trend differentials over untargeted (control) income ranges; the paper states the 'pre-treatment' differential for the 2007-2009 reforms is statistically insignificant at the 5 % level but unstable, which challenges the parallel trends assumption.

key_assumptions.assumption: Income levels outside the range targeted by the reform (the shaded control regions) are unaffected by the reform and can serve as a control group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Panel (a) of Fig. 2 and Fig. B.2, which show the predicted net-of-tax rate changes by income level; the paper notes the 2003 reform's control group is unstable.

population.selection: Hours of work are observed only for employments covered by LON, which covers approximately 50 % of main employments in Denmark (all public employers and all firms with 100+ employees, sampled private firms with 10-100 employees); workers in LON have higher average labor and taxable income than in IDAN. The sample is further conditioned on employment with strictly positive performed hours at t and t+s (intensive margin only), on base-year labor income above 250,000 DKK (2015 level) and on non-missing controls, including twice-lagged income.

identification.source_of_variation: The 2007-2009 reforms: hours trends at income levels targeted by the reform are compared with untargeted control regions, and the reform three-year period is compared with the preceding three-year pre-reform period (2000-2003 vs 2003-2006 for the 2003 reform; 2004-2007 vs 2007-2010 for the 2007-2009 reforms).

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of the reform, hours of work at reform-targeted income levels would have followed the same trend as at untargeted income levels, so the difference in three-year hours changes between the reform and pre-reform periods identifies the reform effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Panel (c) of Fig. 2 and Fig. B.2 show changes in trend differentials over untargeted (control) income ranges; the paper states the 'pre-treatment' differential for the 2007-2009 reforms is statistically insignificant at the 5 % level but unstable, which challenges the parallel trends assumption.

key_assumptions.assumption: Income levels outside the range targeted by the reform (the shaded control regions) are unaffected by the reform and can serve as a control group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Panel (a) of Fig. 2 and Fig. B.2, which show the predicted net-of-tax rate changes by income level; the paper notes the 2003 reform's control group is unstable.

implies_edges.from: tax reform (2003 or 2007-2009)
implies_edges.to: Delta ln h: three-year log change in performed hours of work

key_assumptions.assumption: All trend differentials in hours of performed work between the pre-reform and reform periods are attributed to tax rate changes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the paper lists this attribution, together with the smaller data coverage of LON and measurement error in performed hours, as a source of the high uncertainty of the estimates.

threats_discussed: an unstable 'pre-reform' tax system, which makes the control group questionable for the 2003 reform
a questionable parallel trends assumption, since the pre-treatment differential for the 2007-2009 reforms appears unstable
high uncertainty from the smaller data coverage of LON and measurement error in performed hours of work
attributing all trend differentials between the pre- and post-reform periods to tax rate changes
robustness_checks: Fig. 2 shows the same trend differentials without control variables; the paper states that including control variables leads to minimal changes
unresolved_confounders: the paper states the parallel trends assumption is questionable and that a causal interpretation would be difficult to validate for the 2003 reform because of the unstable control group

heterogeneity.finding: Men (the baseline group) have an elasticity of about 0.05 and women of about 0.14; the paper describes the gender heterogeneity as strong and in line with previous literature.

Fig. 3 reveals strong heterogeneity by education; the paper attributes it partly to lower education levels being associated with lower earnings, which were less targeted by the reforms, and to varying precision of performed hours by education.
Relatively young individuals are estimated to be more responsive than older individuals.
Individuals with young children in the household are more responsive than those without, but with considerable uncertainty in the estimates.
Heterogeneity is otherwise limited and all elasticity estimates are modest, below 0.2.

heterogeneity.finding: Men (the baseline group) have an elasticity of about 0.05 and women of about 0.14; the paper describes the gender heterogeneity as strong and in line with previous literature.

Fig. 3 reveals strong heterogeneity by education; the paper attributes it partly to lower education levels being associated with lower earnings, which were less targeted by the reforms, and to varying precision of performed hours by education.
Relatively young individuals are estimated to be more responsive than older individuals.
Individuals with young children in the household are more responsive than those without, but with considerable uncertainty in the estimates.
Heterogeneity is otherwise limited and all elasticity estimates are modest, below 0.2.
